title: QatarEnergy Extends LNG Force Majeure as Hormuz Closure Deepens Global Energy Crisis
excerpt: The world's largest LNG exporter has extended supply suspensions to India and South Korea through at least mid-September, leasing out tankers into October as renewed Iranian attacks keep the Strait of Hormuz shut.
body:
Key Takeaways
  • QatarEnergy extends LNG supply suspensions to India and South Korea through mid-September, possibly into October.
  • Global LNG supply growth forecast drops from 11% to 1% due to the Strait of Hormuz closure.
  • India faces rising inflation and spot prices as Brent crude surpasses $98 per barrel amid LNG shortages.
  • Pakistan pays record $21.88 per MMBtu for spot LNG, the highest since the 2022 Ukraine crisis.
  • Asian LNG imports decline as countries switch to coal amid soaring prices and supply disruptions.

Force Majeure Extended Through Autumn

QatarEnergy, the world's largest LNG exporter, has extended force majeure declarations on shipments to buyers in India and South Korea, with notices previously set to expire in August and early September now pushed to mid-September, according to trade sources cited by Reuters. Two additional sources said the suspension could stretch into October.

The company has simultaneously begun leasing out vessels from its fleet of nearly 70 LNG carriers on spot deals lasting 30 to 90 days — a move analysts say signals expectations of a prolonged disruption.

"Based on recent fixture reports, at least nine QELM/QET-controlled LNG carriers have been sub-chartered to third parties — including Chevron, BP, EnBW, Cheniere, Kansai, SOCAR, LMCS and Trafigura."

— Ikram Elloumi, Director of Research, Wood Mackenzie

Elloumi noted that QatarEnergy has been chartering vessels despite falling freight rates, suggesting the company is "prioritising fleet utilisation over waiting for a market recovery."

From 11% Growth to 1%: War Rewrites the Supply Outlook

The conflict has erased nearly all projected growth in global LNG supply. Before the war began on February 28, new projects in the US and Canada were expected to boost global LNG output by about 11% year-on-year in 2026. With Qatari and Emirati supply offline, actual growth will be closer to 1%, according to James Taverner, executive director of global gas and LNG research at S&P Global.

Iranian missile strikes during spring 2026 directly hit Ras Laffan LNG Trains 4 and 6, sidelining about 12.8 million tonnes per year of capacity for an estimated three to five years. Pearl GTL Train 2, co-owned by QatarEnergy and Shell, faces a year-long repair outage. Only 26 LNG cargoes have left the Gulf since the conflict began, compared to a pre-war pace of 90 to 100 per month.

The situation worsened this week when Yemen's Houthi rebels attacked Saudi oil tankers in the Red Sea and announced a blockade of the Bab al-Mandab Strait, threatening to shut down a key bypass route for the closed Hormuz chokepoint. Brent crude surged past $98 per barrel on Thursday, while European gas futures hit €62.54 per megawatt hour, the highest in three years.

India Faces Dual Blow: LNG Shortfall and Crude Surge

Before the war, India received almost 60% of its LNG imports from Qatar and the UAE, according to S&P Global price reporter Suyash Pande. That supply has largely evaporated, forcing Indian importers into the volatile spot market.

India emerged as the world's most active long-term LNG buyer in 2025, contracting 8.4 million tonnes per year across six entities including IndianOil, GAIL, and BPCL, according to the International Group of LNG Importers (GIIGNL). The country's eighth LNG import terminal came online last year as part of a plan to nearly double the share of natural gas in its energy mix to 15% over the next decade.

The war has upended those ambitions. The Asian benchmark JKM price surged from about $15 per MMBtu at the start of May to $21.35, its highest since the 2022 Ukraine-related spike. India's Oil Marketing Companies are absorbing losses of ₹20.4 per litre on diesel, and shares in HPCL, Indian Oil, and BPCL fell 1-2.5% on Thursday as crude oil prices climbed.

"Importers heavily affected by the loss of LNG supply included India, Bangladesh and Taiwan, who entered the spot market seeking replacement cargoes."

— Cindy Yeo, S&P Global Price Reporter

The IMF cut India's GDP growth forecast for FY2026/27 by 10 basis points to 6.4% this month, with senior representative Ranil Salgado telling Reuters that the expanding war and its implications for oil prices are among the key downside risks.

Pakistan Paying Record Prices, Asia Scrambles

Pakistan, which historically received nearly all its LNG from Qatar under long-term contracts, has been forced to the spot market at least five times in July alone. The latest purchase — a cargo from TotalEnergies at $21.88 per MMBtu for July 27-28 delivery — marks the highest price Pakistan has paid since the Iran war began and the most expensive spot cargo in four years.

Across the region, demand destruction is already visible. Pakistan's LNG imports have dropped 75%. South Korea's imports are down about 10% year-on-year, with regulators removing caps on coal-fired generation to allow fuel switching. China's LNG imports have fallen 8%, with gas-to-coal switching accelerating there as well.

Buyers Push for New Terms

The crisis is reshaping the global LNG market's power dynamics. Asian and European buyers are pressing Qatar and the UAE for lower prices and stronger supply guarantees in future contracts. Long-term deals that were priced at 12.6-12.7% of Brent crude before the war are now being signed closer to 12.3%, according to industry sources.

China is reportedly in talks to secure long-term supply from exporters that do not rely on the Strait of Hormuz. Edison, Italy's utility, has had Qatari deliveries cancelled from April through early September under force majeure.

For India, the stakes extend beyond immediate supply shortfalls. With European gas storage at just 54% full — compared with 64% at the same point last year — competition for available LNG cargoes heading into the northern hemisphere winter will intensify, keeping prices elevated and adding further pressure to an economy that imports 85% of its crude oil needs.
